newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Scottish Hydro eyes 2x div cover.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Scottish Hydro eyes 2x div cover.

text.p: British electricity generator Scottish Hydro-Electric Plc could see dividend cover fall to around two times from current levels of 2.38 times, chief executive Roger Young told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"I think we've indicated that we would go down towards two...we wouldn't want to go below that in the foreseeable future...two would be the current bottom level," he said.
Scottish Hydro paid out a total dividend for the year of 17.64 pence per share, up 11.9 percent with pretax profits of 205.4 million pounds, a rise of 5.3 percent from a year ago.
Young said the key thing was to ensure that the dividend grew "in a stable way."
Young said the company would be "happy to see interest cover drop towards...four times and that would be gearing in the 80-90 percent range," to fund investments.
Current investment commitments are expected to take gearing to 65 percent from present levels of 52.1 percent by 1999, the company said in its results statement.
Young said projects under consideration were all in electricity generation, including combined heat and power (CHP) plants.
"We have a number of projects around which could use that balance sheet firepower that we've got," he said.
Young said "short term excursions" interest cover of four times and gearing of 90-100 percent would be possible "for the right deal."
He said Scottish Hydro, which expects investments underway currently to increase market share to eight percent by 1999 from about six percent currently, would want to raise that further.
"Eight percent is a step on the road to further increases, providing always that the economics stack up," he said.
Young said that dry weather during the year had cost the company around six million pounds, as low output from its hydro-electric generators had to be topped up by burning coal.

"Because it was quite dry, our hydro output was lower than normal," although better than the previous, extremely dry, year, he said, "we had to burn coal rather than use rainfall to the extent of about six million pounds."
Young said it was too early to tell whether the current year would be hit by dry weather.

He said the company hoped to have "some partnerships" to compete in the domestic electricity supply market which is due to be opened up to competition in 1998, adding that it was "pursuing a number of possible ways into the English market."
It hopes to maintain its market share in Scotland as losses in its monopoly in the north of the country are offset by gains in the south.
But he pointed out that the company was "not pursuing market share we are pursuing profit," and would not enter unprofitable parts of the market.
